title: Stream of Characters
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every word directly per query versus a reversed trie walked backward through the stream.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a StreamChecker that is initialized with a dictionary of words, and supports query(letter), which is called once per streaming character, returning true if some suffix of the stream so far (ending at the most recent character) forms a complete word from the dictionary.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Constructor","Takes a words dictionary"],["query(letter)","Appends letter to the stream, returns true if any suffix of the stream ending here is a dictionary word"],["Goal","Efficiently check stream-ending suffixes using a trie built from REVERSED words"],["Constraints","Up to 2000 total query calls, words up to 200 characters"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Does the stream so far END WITH any dictionary word?\"","Checking a SUFFIX is naturally done by reversing both the words and the direction of the walk, turning it into a prefix check"],["\"Stream arrives one character at a time, repeated queries\"","Buffer the stream and walk BACKWARD from the newest character through a reversed-word trie on each query"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Since checking "does the stream end with word W" is the same as checking "does the REVERSED stream START with reversed W", building a trie from all words REVERSED lets each query walk backward through the buffered stream (from its most recently added character toward older ones) exactly like a normal forward trie prefix walk, stopping successfully the moment an end-of-word marker is reached.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking If a Recording Ends With a Known Jingle, By Playing It Backward
blocks.text: Picture checking whether a live audio stream just ended with one of several short known jingles. Instead of comparing the tail of the recording against each jingle from its start, playing both the jingles and the recent recording BACKWARD turns "ends with" into "starts with", a natural trie prefix check.

blocks.caption: Reverse the words into a trie; walk the stream backward from its newest character to check for a stream-ending match

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: words = ["cd", "f", "kl"], stream = a, b, c, d, e, f, k, l

Results per query: [false,false,false,true,false,true,false,true]. After 'd' the stream ends in "cd", a match. After 'f' the stream ends in just "f", a match. After 'l' the stream ends in "kl", a match.
5. How Should We Think?

Before re-scanning the ENTIRE dictionary against the stream's tail from scratch on every single query (which would be wasteful given up to 2000 queries), notice that reversing the problem direction (reversed words, backward walk) turns "does it end with a dictionary word" into the exact same well-known trie-prefix-walk technique used everywhere else.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "The stream ends with word W" is logically identical to "the REVERSE of the stream starts with the REVERSE of W".

Observation 2: Building a trie from all words reversed, ONCE, at construction time, lets any suffix check become a standard forward trie walk, just walking through the buffered stream from its newest character backward instead of from its oldest character forward.

Observation 3: Each query only needs to append the new letter to a buffer, then walk the reversed trie starting from the buffer's current end, moving toward its start, stopping the instant an end-of-word marker is reached (a match) or a missing trie child is hit (no match).

Observation 4: The buffer never needs to be trimmed for correctness (though it could be, since only the longest word's length worth of recent characters can ever matter), since the backward walk naturally stops early once no further match is possible.
This leads to building a reversed trie from words once, then walking backward through the buffered stream on each query, stopping at the first end-of-word marker reached.
6. Brute Force Solution
Keep the full stream in a buffer. On each query, check directly whether the stream's tail ends with any dictionary word, by comparing suffixes one word at a time.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking endsWith against every word directly implements the definition simply.
This costs O(number of words times word length) per query, wasteful since a reversed trie lets one backward walk check all words sharing a reversed prefix simultaneously.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times average word length) per query.
Space: O(total stream length) for the buffer.
Limitation: a reversed trie shares work across words with common reversed prefixes and stops the backward walk early once no match is possible.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: At construction, reverse every word and insert it into a trie, marking end-of-word nodes exactly as usual. On each query, append the new letter to a buffer, then walk the reversed trie starting from the buffer's LAST character, moving backward (toward earlier characters) one step per trie level. Return true the instant an end-of-word marker is reached; return false if the walk runs out of matching trie children before that.
Build a reversed-word trie once; each query walks backward through the buffered stream via that trie, stopping at the first end-of-word marker or missing child.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run (words reversed: "dc", "f", "lk") for stream ...c,d

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Character read backward","Trie path","End marker?"],"rows":[["1","d (newest)","d","no"],["2","c","d-c","YES, matches reversed \"dc\" = \"cd\", return true"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since a trie built from reversed words checks "does this suffix, read backward, form a prefix of a reversed word" exactly, walking backward from the stream's current end recreates a normal forward trie prefix walk over the reversed characters, correctly detecting whenever the stream's tail exactly forms one of the original words, and stopping early the moment no dictionary word could possibly match any further back.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total word characters) to build, O(longest word length) per query.
Space: O(total word characters) for the trie, O(total stream length) for the buffer.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Stream of Characters is the canonical "check a suffix" trie problem, solved by reversing the direction of both construction and query to reduce it to a familiar prefix walk.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to reverse the words when building the trie (checking prefixes of the original words instead of suffixes of the stream).
Walking the buffered stream FORWARD instead of backward during a query, which checks the wrong end of the stream entirely.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single-character word in the dictionary","Matches on the very query that streams that character."],["No word ever matches any stream suffix","Every query returns false."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "reversing turns a suffix check into a prefix check, which a trie already handles well" demonstrates the key transformation insight for this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "check if a stream ends with any word from a dictionary", think: reverse the words into a trie, then walk the stream backward from its newest character.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you bound the buffer size to only the longest word's length, to avoid unbounded memory growth over a very long stream?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Implement Trie and Short Encoding of Words, other reversed/suffix-oriented trie problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The direct endsWith check costs O(number of words times length) per query; the reversed-trie backward walk costs O(longest word length) per query, the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: reverse the direction of both construction and query to turn a suffix check into a prefix check.
Core Idea: a trie built from reversed words, walked backward from the stream's newest character, detects stream-ending matches efficiently.
Time: O(number of words times length) per query for the brute force, O(longest word length) per query for the trie approach.
Space: O(stream length) for the brute force, O(total word characters plus stream length) for the trie approach.
Most Important Observation: reversing both sides converts an unfamiliar suffix problem into a familiar prefix problem.
Interview Difficulty: a clean trie-design problem with a clever direction-reversal trick.
One line memory trick: reverse the words, walk the stream backward.
